lead: One predictor gives one line. Real answers depend on many things: rent on area and distance, default on income and past dues. Multiple linear regression fits one coefficient per predictor and reads each coefficient with the others held fixed. When the answer is only yes or no, the line bends into an S-shaped logistic curve that predicts a probability. Banks use it for default, hospitals for risk, and apps for click or no click.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for the single-predictor line, least squares and residuals.

blocks.text: Multiple linear regression predicts a numeric response y from k predictors x₁, …, x<sub>k</sub>. For a flat, the response could be monthly rent, with area and distance from the metro as predictors.

blocks.where: y is the response; x₁, …, x<sub>k</sub> are the predictors; β₀ is the intercept; β₁, …, β<sub>k</sub> are the coefficients; ε is the random error.

blocks.text: Least squares chooses the β values that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. A residual is actual y minus predicted y. In matrix form, collect the n observations in a matrix X with one row per observation and a first column of 1s for the intercept. Let y be the column vector of responses. The estimates are β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Xᵀ is the transpose of X, and ⁻¹ is the matrix inverse. The first column of 1s produces the intercept.

Read each coefficient with the other predictors held fixed. If β₁ = 25 for area in square feet, then one extra square foot raises predicted rent by ₹25 when distance is unchanged. This held-fixed clause is the whole meaning of a multiple coefficient.

Categories enter as dummy variables. For a variable with three categories, create two dummies and leave one as the reference. A dummy equals 1 for its category and 0 otherwise. Using three dummies plus an intercept makes the columns dependent, so the matrix inverse fails; this is the dummy-variable trap.

R² is the fraction of the variation in y explained by the fitted model. It lies between 0 and 1; higher is better. R² always rises when any predictor is added, even a useless one, because least squares can always set its coefficient to zero. So compare models with adjusted R².

blocks.where: R²<sub>adj</sub> is adjusted R²; n is the number of observations; k is the number of predictors.

blocks.text: Multicollinearity means predictors are highly correlated with each other. The coefficients remain unbiased, but their standard errors grow and signs can become unstable. Check it with correlation between predictors or variance inflation factor. Do not read a coefficient as a clean isolated effect when this happens.

sections.h3: Logistic regression for a yes-or-no answer

blocks.text: When y is binary (default or no default, pass or fail), a straight line can predict values below 0 or above 1. Logistic regression models the probability p that y = 1. The curve maps any z to a probability between 0 and 1.

blocks.where: p is the probability of success; e is the constant 2.718…; z is the linear score; β₀ is the intercept; β₁ is the coefficient; x is the predictor.

blocks.text: The quantity log(p/(1 − p)) is the logit, and it is linear in x: logit(p) = β₀ + β₁x. The odds of success are p/(1 − p). If β₁ = 0.05, one extra unit of x raises the log-odds by 0.05, so the odds multiply by e^0.05 ≈ 1.051. That is an odds ratio of about 1.05, not a 5 percentage-point rise in probability. Near p = 0.5 the same β₁ moves p a lot; near p = 0.05 it moves p very little.

Maximum likelihood estimates the βs: choose values that make the observed yes/no outcomes most likely. A common rule predicts yes when p ≥ 0.5. Compare predictions with actual outcomes in a confusion matrix, which counts true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives. The figure shows the S-curve and the 0.5 cut-off.

figure.caption: The logistic curve stays between 0 and 1 and crosses the cut-off of 0.5 at score 5, where z = score − 5 = 0.

spec.aria: An S-shaped logistic curve rising from near 0 to near 1 and crossing the horizontal line at 0.5 in the middle.

examples.question: A bank fits logit p = −4 + 0.05 × income, where income is in ₹ thousand and p is the probability that a customer defaults. (a) Find p for an income of ₹80,000. (b) Interpret the coefficient 0.05 as an odds ratio. (c) A rent model is rent = 3000 + 25 × area − 800 × distance, with R² = 0.78, area in square feet and distance in km. State the effect of one extra km of distance with area fixed, and what R² means.
steps: Coefficient 0.05: each extra ₹1,000 raises the log-odds by 0.05, so the odds multiply by e^0.05 = 1.05127, about 5.13% higher odds.
Distance coefficient −800: one km farther from the metro lowers predicted rent by ₹800 when area is held fixed.
R² = 0.78: 78% of the variation in rent is explained by area and distance in this sample.
examples.answer: p = 0.5; the odds ratio is 1.0513, about 5.13% higher odds per extra ₹1,000 of income; one extra km lowers predicted rent by ₹800 with area fixed.
examples.check:
import math
income = 80
z = -4 + 0.05 * income
p = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))
odds_ratio = math.exp(0.05)
percent = (odds_ratio - 1) * 100
rent_drop = 800
print(p)
print(round(odds_ratio, 4))
print(round(percent, 2))
print(rent_drop)

traps: Reading a logistic coefficient as a change in probability. β changes the log-odds; e^β is an odds ratio; the same β moves p a lot near 0.5 and very little near 0.05.
Confusing odds p/(1 − p) with probability p. Odds 2 means p = 2/3, not p = 2.
Thinking a higher R² always means a better model after adding variables. R² always rises; adjusted R² charges a penalty for each predictor.
Reading a multiple coefficient as a one-variable slope. It is partial, with other predictors held fixed; adding a correlated predictor can even flip its sign.
Using k dummies for k categories with an intercept. That creates perfect collinearity; drop one category as the reference.

quiz.q: Write the multiple linear regression model with k predictors and define each symbol.
quiz.a: y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + ⋯ + β<sub>k</sub>x<sub>k</sub> + ε; y is the response, x<sub>j</sub> are predictors, β₀ is the intercept, β<sub>j</sub> are coefficients, and ε is random error.

quiz.q: Why does R² always rise when a predictor is added, and why use adjusted R²?
quiz.a: Least squares can set a useless predictor's coefficient to zero, so the residual sum cannot increase. R² therefore never falls. Adjusted R² penalises each predictor and helps compare models.

quiz.q: A logistic model has logit p = −2 + 0.8x. Find the odds ratio for a one-unit increase in x, and find p at x = 2.5.
A regression of salary on experience and age has R² = 0.85, but both coefficients are negative, while experience alone has a positive slope. Explain.
quiz.a: Experience and age are highly correlated, so multicollinearity is present. The multiple coefficients are partial effects with the other predictor fixed, and unstable signs can appear. The simple slope and the partial slope answer different questions.

quiz.q: What is a dummy variable, and how many dummies are used for a 4-category predictor with an intercept?
quiz.a: A dummy is a 0/1 variable for a category. Use 3 dummies and leave one category as the reference when an intercept is present.

quiz.q: Interpret β = 0.05 in a logistic regression.
quiz.a: A one-unit increase in x raises the log-odds by 0.05. The odds multiply by e^0.05 ≈ 1.051, about 5.1% higher odds. It is not a 5 percentage-point rise in probability.

quiz.q: A confusion matrix has TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130. Compute accuracy and sensitivity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Credit scoring, churn prediction and medical risk models use these two methods daily. Search for logistic regression maximum likelihood, adjusted R², multicollinearity variance inflation factor, and confusion matrix. Regularisation such as ridge and lasso, and ROC curves, are the next tools once these basics are clear.
